summary: Explains how RTP sessions are synchronised and how quickly this can happen. It shows that most sessions synchronise immediately, but video switching conference units or large source-specific multicast groups can add delay, which can be unacceptable for some uses.

eli5.summary: When joining a live video call, your computer has to line up the sound with the picture. This explains how that works and why it can be slow in big groups.

questions: how to synchronise audio and video in rtp
what are the ntp rtp header extensions
subtitle: Ways to line up audio, video and layered streams faster when joining an RTP session.

tldr.problem: A receiver cannot line up the RTP flows of a session until it has received enough RTCP sender reports for each flow. In large source-specific multicast groups or with video switching MCUs, that wait can be too long for layered or multi-description codecs.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6051 lets SSM senders send their first RTCP packet immediately, adds an RTCP-SR-REQ feedback message to ask for a sender report, and defines two RTP header extensions that carry an NTP-format timestamp in-band.
tldr.outcome: All three extensions are backwards compatible. Regular RTCP SR packets must still be sent, and the in-band timestamps also support timestamp-based decoding order recovery for layered codecs.

today: RFC 6051 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2010. It updates RFC 3550, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Synchronisation Delay Problem
sections.content:
Playing audio and video together needs information from RTCP sender report (SR) packets. A receiver cannot synchronise a session until it has enough SR packets for each flow to map each flow's media clock to a common NTP-format reference clock.

Concern had been expressed that this delay is a problem for applications such as those using layered or multi-description video coding. RFC 6051 reviews how synchronisation works, describes the delay to expect, and proposes three backwards compatible extensions: a relaxed RTCP timing rule for SSM senders, a feedback message to request an SR, and RTP header extensions that carry timing in-band. The immediate use case is joining an H.264/SVC session in NI-T mode, but the extensions are not specific to layered coding.
sections.eli5: Matching sound to picture needs clock notes from the sender. Waiting for them can be slow, so this document offers three ways to get them sooner.

sections.title: How RTP Flows Get Synchronised
sections.content:
Receivers synchronise flows using the NTP-format timestamp and the RTP timestamp in RTCP SR packets. The NTP-format timestamps of all flows to be synchronised MUST be sampled from the same clock, while each flow's RTP timestamp comes from its own media clock. Senders and receivers are RECOMMENDED to use a synchronised common reference clock, and how that is signalled is out of scope.

Flows are tied together by the CNAME in RTCP source description packets (or signalled out of band). Senders MUST therefore send periodic compound RTCP packets as required by RFC 3550.

RTCP traffic generally gets 5% of the session bandwidth, with a quarter for active senders and the rest for receivers. A packet is sent about once per reporting interval, randomised between 0.5 and 1.5 times that interval. A 5 second minimum is RECOMMENDED, the initial report MAY be delayed only half that, and for unicast the initial delay MAY be zero. For unicast and for active senders the minimum MAY be scaled to 360 divided by the session bandwidth in kilobits per second.
sections.eli5: Each stream sends clock notes now and then. A receiver matches notes from the sound and the picture to line them up.

sections.title: How Long Initial Synchronisation Takes
sections.content:
Without packet loss, the expected delay is the average time to receive the first RTCP packet in the RTP session with the longest reporting interval. For unicast, senders SHOULD send an initial compound RTCP packet immediately on joining each RTP session, so flows can be synchronised at once unless that packet is lost.

For source-specific multicast (SSM) the delay depends on session bandwidth. The RFC's table, which assumes one sender and a 70 octet average RTCP packet, shows an average of 5.47 seconds at 8 kbps and 0.04 seconds at 4 Mbps. For any-source multicast (ASM) the delay grows with the number of senders. With 10 senders at 8 kbps and 100 receivers it reaches 54.69 seconds. Immediate RTCP is not proposed for ASM because of the risk of an implosion of responses.

Late joiners can wait longer, for three reasons. Fast-start RTCP optimisations apply only at session start. RTCP timing is randomised, so the receiver must estimate clock skew from several reports. Codecs may only start decoding at periodic access points that can be rarer than SR packets.
sections.eli5: If the clock notes come every few seconds, you may wait that long before sound and picture match. In big groups with many senders the wait gets longer.

sections.title: Faster SSM Reports and the Resync Request
sections.content:
Reduced initial interval. In SSM sessions where delay matters, the sender MAY set the delay before its initial compound RTCP packet to zero. This is a local change that can be a configurable option. Receivers sending unicast RTCP feedback MUST NOT use a zero initial delay, and the rules of RFC 5760 apply to them unchanged.

Rapid resynchronisation request. A new RTP/AVPF feedback message, RTCP-SR-REQ, uses FMT = 5. Its feedback control information MUST be empty and its length MUST equal 2. The sender SSRC field identifies the receiver that cannot synchronise, and the media source SSRC identifies the sender whose media it cannot synchronise.

When RFC 4585 is in use, a receiver MAY send it, and a media source that understands it SHOULD send an SR as soon as the early feedback rules allow. The request MAY be repeated once per reporting interval, and the source may ignore it if its regular schedule is soon enough. With unicast feedback in SSM, a feedback target that is not the media source should forward the request, by a mechanism the RFC does not define.
sections.eli5: A sender may speak up the moment it joins. A listener who missed the clock note can also ask, "please send that again."

sections.title: In-Band Timestamps in RTP Header Extensions
sections.content:
Using the header extension mechanism of RFC 5285, an RTP packet can carry an OPTIONAL NTP-format timestamp. It MUST correspond to the same instant as the packet's RTP timestamp and MUST come from the same clock as the NTP timestamps in RTCP SR packets. A receiver that knows the SSRC to CNAME mapping can use it exactly as if another SR packet had arrived.

Two variants exist. Variant A carries the full 64-bit timestamp from RFC 5905. Variant B carries the lower 24 bits of the seconds plus the 32 bits of fraction, and then RTCP sender reports MUST supply the upper 8 bits of the seconds.

The extension MAY be put in any packets, is RECOMMENDED for timestamp-based decoding order recovery, and SHOULD be sent in packets at a video random access point and the associated audio packets. Regular RTCP SR packets MUST still be sent, for receivers that follow RFC 3550 and for cases where middleboxes strip the extension. In SDP, the extensions are signalled with the URIs urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:ntp-64 and urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:ntp-56. Using them can greatly improve IPTV channel surfing and some interactive video conferencing, but they reduce the efficiency of RTP header compression.
sections.eli5: Instead of sending clock notes separately, the sender can stick a tiny clock label on some video packets. Your device reads the label and matches sound and picture straight away.

sections.title: Decoding Order Recovery for Layered Codecs
sections.content:
Layered, multi-description and multi-view codecs split media across several RTP flows, for example H.264 SVC in NI-T mode and MPEG surround audio. Higher-layer flows often cannot be decoded until the matching data in lower layers has been decoded.

For rapid and accurate synchronisation, the sender SHOULD insert the header extensions synchronously into all component flows, for packets from exactly the same sampling instant, so they carry identical NTP-format timestamps. The RFC RECOMMENDS doing this at least once per random access point. The sender MUST keep sending RTCP SR packets that are consistent with the in-band mapping, and receivers are RECOMMENDED to sanity check both sources and discard outliers.

The decoding hierarchy MUST be signalled out of band, for example with RFC 5583. Each flow MUST contain packets for all the sampling instants of the flows it depends on, and the sender MUST generate extra packets if needed (an Empty NAL unit packet for H.264 SVC). The receiver derives an NTP-format timestamp for each packet, groups packets with identical timestamps, handles groups in ascending timestamp order, and passes each group's packets to the decoder from the base flow upward. It will have to buffer packets because decoding order need not match transmission order.
sections.eli5: Layered video is like a stack of transparent sheets. You need the bottom sheet first, so matching clock labels let you stack the right sheets from the same moment.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3550, RFC 4585 and RFC 5285 apply.

When a session uses SRTP (RFC 3711), the new header extension is not part of the encrypted portion of the RTP or RTCP packets, whereas those NTP-format timestamps are encrypted when SRTP is used without the extension. The RFC calls this a minor information leak that is not believed to be significant. Middleboxes that do not understand the extensions may remove them or fail to update them.
sections.eli5: The clock label rides outside the locked part of a protected stream, so others could read it. The authors think that matters very little.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered one new value in the FMT table for RTPFB payload types: RTCP-SR-REQ, long name RTCP Rapid Resynchronisation Request, value 5.

IANA also registered two RTP compact header extensions from RFC 5285: urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:ntp-64 for the 64-bit timestamp format and urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:ntp-56 for the 56-bit format.
sections.eli5: The new message type and the two label styles were added to the official lists so everyone uses the same names.
